title: American jazz records reach Berlin and affect his style
summary: Records by Nichols, the Wolverines, Trumbauer, Henderson and Ellington arrived; Briggs says they influenced but did not change his style, and he played around the melody for patrons.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Now, this was also the time that you were buying all those records.
Briggs
Yes.
Records were beginning to come over from the States; is that right?

Yes, yes. Recordings started coming over, and the orchestras started being pretty popular. And you had -- Red Nichols was already on the scene. The Wolverines were on the scene. Frankie Trumbauer came on the scene. And about the same time with Fletcher Henderson and the Duke was just beginning.
Right, this is say '27.
Yes, yes. So, I don't think I'm being arrogant in saying that I think I helped, because I was on the spot, I was present, you see. I think I helped to push everything, 'cause I was there on the spot.
Briggs
(Tape 3-February 26, 1982)
We have been talking about the early arrival of American Jazz records into Europe, particularly into Berlin where Mr. Briggs was working at that time in 1927.
Well, let me ask you this, then, did your own style change as you began to hear these new records, did it have an effect on you?
To a certain extent it did. To a certain extent it did. It was not a direct copy.
Yeh.
Not a direct copy, but it was just certain influence, that is I was trying to find my path between what I heard and what I felt myself.
Right.
And I think it works out pretty well, because at the time, in those days, you were supposed to play around the
Briggs 186
melody, and not get away too far from the melody.
And as you had -- we had certain other bands, you've probably heard of Art Hickman's band --
Sure.
Art Hickman's band, who had a wonderful trumpet player, Clancy Williams, --
Clancy Williams.
Clancy Williams, right.

He was a wonderful trumpet player who I met in Paris, the few days when I was with Jenkins, because we played in the same establishment, for a couple of hours, and that -- we had to amend our way of playing and just don't leave the melody, and just play around the melody, so that the patrons will understand what you're doing.
In Germany if they didn't understand it, they say it's "cat's music".
Briggs
Cat's music?
Yes.
Right.
You see. So, we had to -- with that influence, we realized then that the influence was almost the same in the States as we were doing, the same as we were doing, it was happening in America, you see.
